signal.title: promql: make duplicate series error message deterministic
signal.text: ## What This makes the PromQL many-to-many duplicate-series error deterministic: `found duplicate series for the match group ... [X, Y] ...` `VectorBinop` now sorts the two duplicate series label strings before formatting the error. The error text and semantics are otherwise unchanged. ## Why this site, not the map iteration upstream The two series strings were previously rendered from `rs.Metric.String()` and `duplSample.Metric.String()` in whichever order the duplicate pair arrived from `rightSigs`. That order can be influenced by Go map iteration randomization upstream (the RHS Matrix is assembled by iterating `seriess map[uint64]seriesAndTimestamp` in `rangeEval` / `rangeEvalAgg`), even though normal `Matrix` result order is already sorted by `sortMatrixResult` before being returned to clients. The only place the non-determinism leaks out is this error path, so the smallest fix is to sort the two rendered label strings immediately before formatting the error. Full reproducer and root-cause walk in #18809. The error string itself was last touched on 2021-11-17 in commit 5d4db805 and has otherwise stayed stable for years, so this keeps the existing message format intact. ## Test Added a `.test` regression case in `promql/promqltest/testdata/operators.test` that asserts the many-to-many error renders the duplicate pair in sorted order. Added `TestManyToManyErrorDeterministic` in `promql/engine_test.go`, which repeatedly evaluates the offending query and asserts every rendered error message is byte-identical, pinning the stable `(A, B)` output regardless of whether the underlying duplicate pair is encountered as `(A, B)` or `(B, A)`. Verified by temporarily reverting the sort: both tests FAIL with the unsorted ordering; restoring the patch makes them PASS. ## Which issue(s) does the PR fix: Fixes #18809. Also unblocks cortexproject/cortex#7546 (a flaky test in Cortex caused by this exact non-determinism — tactical downstream workaround in cortexproject/cortex#7550 can be removed once this lands and is vendored). ## Does this PR introduce a user-facing change? No behavior change. The error message content is unchanged; only the ordering of the two label strings inside the existing `[X, Y]` brackets is now stable. ```release-notes [BUGFIX] PromQL: Make the "found duplicate series for the match group" many-to-many matching error message deterministic by sorting the two duplicate labels. ```

signal.title: discovery/aws: describe each ElastiCache cluster only once
signal.text: `describeCacheClusters` issues two `DescribeCacheClusters` queries for every page (and for every configured cluster ID), one with `ShowCacheClustersNotInReplicationGroups` set to `false` and one with it set to `true`, then concatenates both responses. Per the [API reference](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonElastiCache/latest/APIReference/API_DescribeCacheClusters.html), those two responses overlap rather than partition: > Returns information about all provisioned clusters if no cluster identifier is specified [...] > > **ShowCacheClustersNotInReplicationGroups** — An optional flag that can be included in the `DescribeCacheCluster` request to show only nodes (API/CLI: clusters) that are not members of a replication group. In practice, this means Memcached and single node Valkey or Redis OSS clusters. The unfiltered response already lists every provisioned cluster, and the filtered one is a strict subset of it. Every cluster that is not a replication group member is therefore returned by both queries and described twice. Replication group members are unaffected, which is why the duplication is invisible to anyone running only those. Consequences: - Each standalone cluster produces two identical entries in the target group, doubling `prometheus_sd_discovered_targets` and listing the cluster twice on the `/service-discovery` page. - The duplicated ARNs reach `listTagsForResource`, which starts one goroutine per slice entry, so `ListTagsForResource` is called twice for every standalone cluster. - Half of the `DescribeCacheClusters` calls are redundant. Scraping itself is unaffected: `scrapePool.sync` keys `uniqueLoops` by `Target.hash()`, so identical targets collapse into one scrape loop. The fix leaves `ShowCacheClustersNotInReplicationGroups` unset and issues a single query per page or cluster ID. The mock ignored the flag, which is why no existing test caught this; it now filters the way the API documents it. The first commit adds a test that fails without the fix. I do not have an AWS account with a Memcached or single node cluster to confirm this end to end, so the change rests on the documented behaviour of the flag. ```release-notes [BUGFIX] AWS SD: Describe each ElastiCache cluster once instead of twice for clusters that are not replication group members. ```

signal.title: tsdb/index: fix data race in memposting
signal.text: Fixes: #15317 ## What This refactors `MemPostings` to safely handle concurrent readers and out-of-order insertions by tracking which portion of each postings list may already be visible to readers. Instead of always copying an entire postings list when repairing an ordering violation, the implementation now performs in-place repairs whenever it is safe, falling back to copying only when readers could observe the modified region. The change also introduces sharded read tracking, preserves the fast path for in-order appends, restores regression tests, and fixes the race condition that could cause queries to return incorrect series. ## Why Previously, `MemPostings` repaired ordering violations by modifying postings lists in place after readers had already obtained references to them, introducing a data race and allowing readers to observe incorrectly ordered postings. An earlier fix resolved the race by copying the entire postings list on every repair, but this caused excessive memory allocations and was reverted due to poor performance. By tracking the portion of each list that may be visible to readers, this implementation copies only when necessary, eliminating the race while avoiding the significant memory and performance overhead of unconditional whole-list copies. <!-- - Please give your PR a title in the form "area: short description". signal.title: tsdb: fix OOO chunk ID overflow via modular wrapping
signal.text: #### Which issue(s) does the PR fix: Ref: https://github.com/grafana/mimir/issues/4541 #### Release notes for end users (**ALL** commits must be considered). *Reviewers should verify clarity and quality.* ```release-notes [BUGFIX] TSDB: Fix out-of-order chunk ID overflow by wrapping `firstOOOChunkID` modulo 2^23 instead of growing unbounded. ``` ## Summary Fix unbounded growth of `firstOOOChunkID` in the OOO chunk path. When a series accumulates enough OOO chunk truncation cycles, the counter eventually overflows the 23-bit ID space, causing a panic in `NewHeadChunkRef` and query failures from index-out-of-range in `oooChunk`. The fix applies modular arithmetic (bitmask wrapping) at the three sites that produce or consume OOO chunk IDs: - `oooHeadChunkID()`: mask the packed position to 23 bits before setting the OOO flag - `oooChunk()`: use modular subtraction (`& (oooChunkIDMask - 1)`) instead of signed subtraction to recover the slice index - `truncateChunksBefore()`: wrap `firstOOOChunkID` with `& (oooChunkIDMask - 1)` after incrementing ### Context The existing guard in `mmapCurrentOOOHeadChunk` caps the number of *active* OOO chunks per series at `oooChunkIDMask - 1`, but it does not prevent `firstOOOChunkID` from growing without bound across repeated truncation cycles. Aliasing safety across the wrap boundary is guaranteed by the OOO isolation mechanism (`oooIsolationState`), which prevents truncation of chunks while a reader holds a reference. A design document with full correctness reasoning, locking invariant diagrams, and the test plan is available here: https://gist.github.com/periklis/f6bbcdd9cdff32a8fbb36f8d09f412d8

signal.title: scrape: keep staleness tracking in sync when the series ref changes
signal.text: Follow up on #19325. Staleness is tracked in `scrapeCache.seriesCur`/`seriesPrev`, both keyed by `storage.SeriesRef`. When the storage hands out a new reference for a series it already gave one for (e.g. it was garbage collected and had to be recreated), the scrape loop updates the cached reference and tracks the current scrape under the new one, while the previous scrape is still tracked under the old one. The old reference is then missing from the current scrape, so `forEachStale` reports the series as stale even though the target still exposes it. The stale marker is appended for `ce.ref`, i.e. for the *new*, live reference, at the same timestamp as the sample of this scrape. `headAppender.Commit` writes the WAL before applying samples to the head, so while the head itself drops the marker as a duplicate, it is already persisted: ``` StaleNaN append at same t returned err=<nil> WAL sample: ref=1 t=1000 v=1 stale=false WAL sample: ref=1 t=1000 v=NaN stale=true ``` Remote write and agent mode read the WAL, so they ship the marker downstream and the series ends there until the next scrape. This affects appender v2 since the reference was first written back to the cache, and appender v1 since #19325 made it consistent with v2. v2 is what the Prometheus binary runs today (`cmd/prometheus/main.go` passes `nil, fanoutStorage` to `scrape.NewManager`), so the fix is done for both loops. `scrapeCache.updateRef` now re-keys the staleness tracking to the new reference, and both scrape loops go through it. It deliberately *moves* the tracking instead of dropping it: dropping it would suppress the stale marker of a series that is still exposed but stopped being tracked for another reason in the same scrape, which would make staleness depend on whether the reference happened to change. The one case where that is observable is a series that starts carrying an explicit timestamp, which the last two test cases pin down. ### Tests `TestScrapeLoopCacheRefUpdatedOnChange` from #19325 is reworked into the table driven `TestScrapeLoopSeriesRefChange`, which drives a sequence of scrapes and asserts on the samples the scrape loop appends, not only on the cached reference. It reuses the `teststorage.Appendable` mock with an injected reference rather than a purpose built appendable, which is what makes the stale marker visible. All cases run against both scrape loops: | case | before | after | | --- | --- | --- | | reference stays the same | pass | pass | | reference changes while the series is still exposed | stale marker | pass | | reference changes on every scrape | stale marker per change | pass | | series stops being exposed after the reference changed | extra stale marker | pass | | explicit timestamp appears, reference stays the same | pass | pass | | explicit timestamp appears and the reference changes | pass | pass | The last two agree by construction, which is what keeps `updateRef` from turning into a plain delete. Commit 2 adds the test and fails on purpose, commit 3 fixes the bug. ```release-notes [BUGFIX] Scrape: Do not append a stale marker for a series that is still exposed when the storage returns a new series reference for it. ```

signal.title: promtool: Fixed tsdb dump silently dropping first samples of histogram series.
signal.text: #### Which issue(s) does the PR fix: None. #### Does this PR introduce a user-facing change? ```release-notes [BUGFIX] promtool: Fixed `tsdb dump` silently dropping native histogram samples. ``` `promtool tsdb dump` silently drops all native histogram and float histogram samples. The `formatSeriesSet` function used three sequential `for` loops, each calling `it.Next()` as its loop condition. When loop 1 exits (eg because the series contains histogram data, not float), `it.Next()` has already advanced the iterator past the first histogram sample. Loop 2 then calls `it.Next()` again, skipping that sample entirely. The same problem occurs between loop 2 and loop 3. The fix replaces the three sequential loops with a single loop and a `switch` on the value type returned by `it.Next()`. This matches the correct iterator pattern used elsewhere in the codebase (e.g. `tsdb/chunks/chunks.go`, `scrape/scrape_test.go`). A test has been added.

signal.text: `prometheus_sd_last_update_timestamp_seconds` is a `GaugeVec` labelled by the SD config set name, set together with `prometheus_sd_discovered_targets` in `allGroups()`. signal.title: discovery/aws: don't panic on ElastiCache resources with absent optional fields
signal.text: None of the members of the SDK's `ServerlessCache` and `CacheCluster` types are marked required - `elasticache v1.56.4` carries zero `This member is required` annotations on either - but the ElastiCache discovery dereferences nine of them with no nil check, all inside the `model.LabelSet` literals: ```go labels := model.LabelSet{ elasticacheLabelDeploymentOption: model.LabelValue("serverless"), elasticacheLabelServerlessCacheARN: model.LabelValue(*cache.ARN), elasticacheLabelServerlessCacheName: model.LabelValue(*cache.ServerlessCacheName), ... } ``` A cache returned without one of them panics, and since nothing under `discovery/` recovers, that takes down the whole Prometheus process. The fields further down in the same two functions are already guarded, so this reads as an oversight in the literals rather than a deliberate assumption. Guarded here, following the pattern the surrounding code already uses: - `ServerlessCache`: `ARN`, `ServerlessCacheName`, `Status`, `Engine`, `FullEngineVersion`, `MajorEngineVersion` - `CacheCluster`: `ARN`, `CacheClusterId`, `CacheClusterStatus` `ARN` additionally keys the tag lookup. Resources without one are skipped when collecting the ARNs to describe tags for, and the lookup goes through `aws.ToString`, so a missing ARN yields no tags instead of a panic. **On the first commit.** Writing a test that drives `refresh()` with both deployment options populated exposed a data race: the two errgroup goroutines each append to the same `targetgroup.Group` with no synchronisation. No existing test covered that combination, which is why it went unnoticed. CI runs the suite with `-race`, so this had to be fixed before the test could land, and it is separated into its own commit. The second commit adds the test and fails; the third adds the guards. ```release-notes [BUGFIX] AWS SD: Do not panic when the ElastiCache API omits optional fields of a serverless cache or cache cluster. ```

signal.title: discovery/kubernetes: fall back to status.loadBalancer.ingress for service loadbalancer IP
signal.text: ### Summary `__meta_kubernetes_service_loadbalancer_ip` was always empty for LoadBalancer services on Kubernetes 1.24+ clusters because it read only `spec.loadBalancerIP`, which was deprecated in that release. Modern cloud providers (GKE, EKS, AKS, MetalLB, ...) now populate `status.loadBalancer.ingress` and leave `spec.loadBalancerIP` unset. ### Problem In `discovery/kubernetes/service.go`: ```go if svc.Spec.Type == apiv1.ServiceTypeLoadBalancer { labelSet[serviceLoadBalancerIP] = lv(svc.Spec.LoadBalancerIP) } ``` `spec.loadBalancerIP` is always `""` on Kubernetes 1.24+ unless the user sets it explicitly, so `__meta_kubernetes_service_loadbalancer_ip` is always blank when using relabelling such as `__meta_kubernetes_service_loadbalancer_ip` as a `__param_target` for blackbox-style probes. ### Solution When `spec.loadBalancerIP` is empty, fall back to the first entry in `status.loadBalancer.ingress` — first the `.IP` field, then `.Hostname` if no IP is available. The spec field is still checked first to keep backward compatibility for clusters that still set it. ```go loadBalancerIP := svc.Spec.LoadBalancerIP if loadBalancerIP == "" && len(svc.Status.LoadBalancer.Ingress) > 0 { if ip := svc.Status.LoadBalancer.Ingress[0].IP; ip != "" { loadBalancerIP = ip } else { loadBalancerIP = svc.Status.LoadBalancer.Ingress[0].Hostname } } labelSet[serviceLoadBalancerIP] = lv(loadBalancerIP) ``` ### Testing - Added `makeLoadBalancerServiceWithStatusIngressIP()` helper and `TestServiceDiscoveryLoadBalancerIPFromStatusIngress` test that verifies `__meta_kubernetes_service_loadbalancer_ip` is populated from `status.loadBalancer.ingress[0].IP` when `spec.loadBalancerIP` is empty. - All existing tests unchanged and passing locally. Fixes #14398

signal.title: scrape: go test -shuffle aborts the test run with "select on synctest channel from outside bubble"
signal.text: Root cause is upstream in Go's `net`, which I reported as golang/go#80903. It needs a change here regardless: the upstream fix covers two of the three channels involved, and the third is the one this hits on the default resolver path. ### What did you do? Ran the `scrape` package's own tests with Go's test shuffling enabled, on a clean checkout of `main` at `7a73c9ae6`: ``` go test -count=1 -shuffle=42 ./scrape/ ``` ### What did you expect to see? The same result as the default order, which passes. ### What did you see instead? Under which circumstances? The run aborts. No test is reported as failing — the process is gone first: ``` fatal error: select on synctest channel from outside bubble goroutine 2196 [running]: net.cgoLookupIP ← net.(*Resolver).lookupIP ← internal/singleflight.(*Group).doCall created by internal/singleflight.(*Group).DoChan in goroutine 1823 FAIL github.com/prometheus/prometheus/scrape 1.745s ``` `-shuffle` appears in no workflow, so the default order is the only one CI runs, which is why this passes upstream on every commit. Nine tests in this package reach `osutil.GetFQDN`, and the fatal needs the `synctest` one — `TestScrapeOffsetDistribution`, through `setOffsetSeed` — to be the **first** lookup in the process; once an outside caller has reached the resolver, the in-bubble one is harmless. Measured two ways: each of the other eight can abort when paired with it, and on one such pair ten seeds split cleanly by which test ran first. It is not the `singleflight` group the stack trace suggests: the object is a package-level channel in `net`, created lazily under a `sync.Once`, so whoever calls first decides which bubble it belongs to for the rest of the process. The full write-up is in golang/go#80903. `manager.go:390-393` already describes the hazard, and `setupSynctestManager` avoids it with a fake server, a `net.Pipe` per dial and `skipJitterOffsetting`. `TestScrapeOffsetDistribution` is the one `synctest` site that doesn't go through the helper, and the lookup isn't in the scraping path a fake network covers: it arrives from `ApplyConfig` → `setOffsetSeed`. Setting the existing flag on that test isn't a way out on its own: ``` --- FAIL: TestScrapeOffsetDistribution scrape_test.go:8033: "1" is not greater than "2" Expected targets to be scraped at staggered offsets rather than simultaneously at scrape index 0 ``` The flag does two things at once: it skips the seed calculation, and at `scrape.go:1313` it zeroes each scrape loop's offset — which is what that test asserts. The three tests using the helper depend on the second effect; this one needs the first and cannot have the second. Fixing it here does not depend on the upstream fix landing: the third channel, `net.threadLimit`, derives its capacity from `rlim.Cur`, so it cannot simply be created eagerly, and with the other two changed the default resolver path on this platform still aborts. Related: `#17941`, though the mechanism there is different. ### System information ``` darwin/arm64, go1.26.1 ``` ### Prometheus version ``` Reproduced from source at 7a73c9ae6, not from a release binary. ``` ### Prometheus configuration file ``` n/a — this is a test-suite failure, no configuration involved. ```

signal.title: scrape: avoid a full-body copy of every scrape response
signal.text: A scrape can hold two full copies of the response body on the heap. This PR removes the second copy. @krajorama you reviewed #19282 in `model/textparse`, and @bwplotka / @bboreham for the `scrape` side: would one of you have time to look? Happy to split the two commits into separate PRs if that is easier to review. ## The problem `scrapeLoop.scrapeAndReport` takes a buffer from a pool sized to the previous body size, wraps it in a `bytes.Buffer`, fills it with `ReadFrom`, and hands the result to the parser: ```go b = sl.buffers.Get(sl.lastScrapeSize).([]byte) buf = bytes.NewBuffer(b) readResponse(..., buf) // -> buf.ReadFrom(body) <-- copy 1 b = buf.Bytes() app.append(b, ...) // -> NewPromParser: append(b, '\n') <-- copy 2 ``` There are two independent places a full-body reallocation can happen: 1. **`bytes.Buffer.ReadFrom`** calls `grow(bytes.MinRead)` before *every* `Read`. If fewer than `bytes.MinRead` (512) bytes of spare capacity remain once the body has been read in full, that `grow` calls `growSlice`, which **doubles the buffer and copies the whole body**. 2. **The parser's line terminator.** `NewPromParser` does `append(b, '\n')` unconditionally. When `cap(b) == len(b)` this reallocates and copies the whole body, and the copy is **retained for as long as the parser lives**. Both are guaranteed for bodies larger than the pool's biggest bucket. `pool.New(1e3, 100e6, 3, ...)` generates buckets of `1000 * 3^k`, so the largest is **59049000 (~59 MB)**; above that `pool.Get` falls through to `p.make(sz)` and returns an **exact-sized** slice with `cap == len`. ## Which copy you get depends on the transport Only responses with a `Content-Length` return the final bytes and `io.EOF` together, and so skip `ReadFrom`'s last `grow`. Measured over a real HTTP connection with an 8 MiB body, driving `targetScraper.readResponse` and `NewPromParser`: | transport | slack=0 | slack=1 | slack=512 | |---|---|---|---| | Content-Length | parser copy (~1.25N) | clean | clean | | chunked | read copy (2N) | read copy (2N) | clean | | gzip | read copy (2N) | read copy (2N) | clean | `ScrapeConfig.EnableCompression` defaults to `true`, so gzip is the common case in practice. Worth calling out: **a single spare byte is not sufficient.** It is the `bytes.MinRead` threshold that matters, not merely having `cap > len`. ## The change **Commit 1 (`scrape`)** asks the pool for `bytes.MinRead` more than the last body size. This closes both sites at once: it satisfies `ReadFrom`'s final `grow`, and it keeps `cap > len` for the parser. Bucket selection only changes when the previous body size falls within 512 bytes *below* a bucket boundary. Buckets are a factor of 3 apart, so this is rare (~0.004% for the 19683000 bucket), and out-of-pool allocations simply grow by 512 bytes. Bodies that sit comfortably inside a bucket already had spare capacity and are unaffected. **Commit 2 (`textparse`)** skips the terminator append when the body already ends in a newline. The exposition format requires a trailing newline, so for a well-formed body the append exists only to serve the malformed case, yet it costs a full-body copy for any caller that passes an exact-sized slice. Bodies without a trailing newline, and empty bodies, are terminated exactly as before. The two commits are independent; commit 1 is the one that matters for scrapes. ## Benchmarks `scrape` (new `BenchmarkScrapeLoopScrapeAndReportLargeBody`; the loop's default pool tops out at 729000 bytes, so a few MiB reproduces the out-of-pool condition at a practical size): ``` │ before │ after │ │ B/op │ B/op vs base │ ScrapeLoopScrapeAndReport/appV2=false 160.8Ki ± 1% 160.8Ki ± 1% ~ ScrapeLoopScrapeAndReport/appV2=true 416.5Ki ± 0% 416.5Ki ± 0% ~ ScrapeLoopScrapeAndReportLargeBody/1MiB 3.784Mi ± 1% 2.547Mi ± 0% -32.68% ScrapeLoopScrapeAndReportLargeBody/4MiB 14.89Mi ± 1% 10.05Mi ± 1% -32.51% ScrapeLoopScrapeAndReportLargeBody/16MiB 59.77Mi ± 1% 40.01Mi ± 0% -33.07% │ sec/op │ sec/op vs base │ ScrapeLoopScrapeAndReportLargeBody/1MiB 7.666m ± 5% 6.942m ± 7% -9.44% ScrapeLoopScrapeAndReportLargeBody/4MiB 38.28m ± 6% 35.92m ± 3% -6.18% ScrapeLoopScrapeAndReportLargeBody/16MiB 214.9m ± 3% 202.9m ± 3% -5.55% ``` The pre-existing benchmarks use a ~190 KB body that lands in a 243000-byte bucket, so they already had slack and are unchanged, as expected. `textparse` (new `BenchmarkNewPromParser`): ``` │ before │ after │ │ B/op │ B/op vs base │ NewPromParser/exact-sized 246544 ± 0% 784.0 ± 0% -99.68% NewPromParser/exact-sized/no-trailing-nl 240.8Ki ± 0% 240.8Ki ± 0% ~ NewPromParser/spare-capacity 784.0 ± 0% 784.0 ± 0% ~ │ allocs/op │ allocs/op vs base │ NewPromParser/exact-sized 4.000 ± 0% 3.000 ± 0% -25.00% ``` ## Tests - `TestScrapeLoopBodyBufferSlack` asserts the scrape read buffer keeps at least `bytes.MinRead` spare capacity, across in-bucket, exactly-at-the-boundary, and out-of-pool body sizes. It fails on `main` for the three out-of-pool cases. - `TestPromParserLineTerminator` asserts a body with and without a trailing newline parses identically, that an exact-sized body ending in a newline is not copied, and that bodies without one (and empty bodies) are still terminated. `go test ./scrape/... ./model/textparse/...` and `golangci-lint run` are clean. #### Which issue(s) does the PR fix: Fixes #19395 #### Release notes for end users (**ALL** commits must be considered). ```release-notes [PERF] Scrape: Avoid copying the whole response body an extra time on every scrape. ```
